claims.text: No gluten-free handling or cross-contamination protocols are documented; the seasoned, soy-based dishes most likely contain wheat-derived soy sauce/seasonings, so gluten should be assumed present.
Standard Japanese soy sauce and miso-based seasonings are used in the plate; there is no mention of wheat-free tamari, so wheat is likely present in the seasoning.
The kitchen is entirely plant-based, so there is no meat, fish, or egg cross-contact in the dishes.

Reservations are required and dishes are made to order, so allergy needs are best raised in advance by phone or email; however, the menu is mainly Japanese-only and only a little English is spoken, which can make detailed allergy communication harder.
Fully vegan kitchen with no animal products used, removing any risk of meat, fish, egg, or dairy cross-contact.
Vegetables are pesticide-free / reduced-pesticide and sourced from trusted local farmers, with a strong seasonal, ingredient-led focus.
Soy sauce / seasoning ingredients are not disclosed; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so a gluten-sensitive diner must ask whether the dipping sauce and any soy sauce are wheat-free.
Reviewers report the yudofu dipping sauce is fish-based (not vegan); a strict vegan should decline the standard dipping sauce and ask which condiments are plant-based.
An English menu is available but staff speak limited English; a written Japanese allergy note is recommended for clear communication about sauce and dashi.
A temple shojin-style kitchen centred on tofu and vegetables, so meat and most animal cross-contact is inherently low — the main animal-derived risk is the dipping sauce rather than the food itself.

The menu is wheat-heavy (wheat gluten/fu, tempura, vegetable pakora), and fried items share oil, so cross-contact with gluten is effectively unavoidable for a strict GF diner. No dedicated fryer is documented.
Standard Japanese cooking using soy sauce; no wheat-free/tamari soy sauce is advertised, so assume the soy sauce contains wheat.

Reviewers report everything is vegan except one clearly-labeled cake containing egg and dairy; that single dairy/egg dessert is the only animal product in the room, so cross-contact with meat, fish or dashi is minimal.
Family-run with a single fixed set menu and no English menu or English-speaking staff, so accommodating specific allergies on the spot is limited; communicate needs in Japanese in advance.
Essentially a fully plant-based kitchen built on organic local Uji vegetables and brown rice, so vegans can order the set with confidence and very low risk of animal-product cross-contact.
Uses organic produce from nearby farmers, house-made tempeh, and self-roasted coffee, with vegan cakes/tarts also available.

name: ソーシャル・キッチン（Social Kitchen） (Social Kitchen)

claims.text: The kitchen is not fully vegan and rotates among different operators by day, so animal ingredients may be used on the same equipment depending on who is cooking; confirm with the day's operator.
Plant-based dishes (such as a vegan South Indian bean curry) have been part of the café's offering, and the venue's ethos centers on local ingredients and low-waste cooking.

name: 素食カフェ Ren 四条大宮店 (Soshoku Cafe Ren Shijo Omiya)

claims.text: Menu is built around soy-meat mock dishes, tempura and baked goods (curry bun, apple cake) that typically contain wheat, so shared frying and wheat cross-contact are likely; no gluten-free handling is advertised.
Seasoning likely uses standard Japanese soy sauce (usually wheat-containing); the sources do not confirm a wheat-free tamari, so a gluten-free diner should ask.
The kitchen is fully plant-based, using no meat, fish, eggs or dairy at all, which removes animal cross-contact risk for vegan diners.

Completely animal-product-free kitchen following Buddhist 'su si' principles, with food also free of the five pungent vegetables (onion, garlic, leek, green onion, chives) and made from pesticide-free, self-grown produce.
Counter seating makes it easy and comfortable for a solo vegan/vegetarian traveler to dine.

name: タローベーカリー (Taro Bakery)

claims.text: This is a wheat bakery: domestic wheat flour is used throughout and is handled across the whole kitchen, so flour cross-contact is unavoidable. Not suitable for celiac or gluten-sensitive diners.
Vegan loaves are baked in the same kitchen as breads that contain dairy/egg, so shared-equipment cross-contact is possible. Ask staff which specific items are fully plant-based that day.
The owners deliberately put out egg-free, dairy-free and sugar-free items every day for vegans and people with allergies, indicating allergy awareness — though communication is in Japanese.
The plain/base bread is genuinely vegan, made from only Hokkaido wheat, natural yeast, salt and water — no butter, oil, milk, egg or sugar.
Emphasis on safe, simple ingredients and locally grown pesticide-free vegetables in the sandwiches.

No information is published on whether the soy sauce, dressings, or simmering liquids are wheat-free; standard Japanese soy sauce used in temple cooking normally contains wheat, so gluten-sensitive diners should assume wheat is present unless confirmed.

This is a fully plant-based shojin ryori kitchen run by a Zen temple, so by religious practice no meat or fish is used — there is no animal cross-contact in the cooking, a strong baseline for vegan diners.
Meals are prepared by the abbot himself, a published shojin cookbook author, with documented all-vegetable menus (e.g., shiraae tofu dressings, simmered vegetables, furofuki daikon, azuki porridge).

name: ヴィーガンラーメン ウズ キョウト (Vegan Ramen UZU KYOTO)

claims.text: All ramen noodles are made with wheat flour (Hokkaido flour plus organic whole-grain flour from Aya, Miyazaki), so the kitchen routinely handles wheat/gluten and is not suitable for celiac diners.
The signature ramen uses soy sauce; sources do not specify whether it is wheat-free (tamari), so assume standard wheat-containing soy sauce unless confirmed with staff.
The entire restaurant is fully vegan, so there is no meat, fish or dairy in the kitchen and no animal-product cross-contact. The broth uses kelp and shiitake rather than animal dashi.

Reviewers describe staff as friendly and knowledgeable, explaining dishes and even offering descriptions in other languages; no formal allergy protocol is documented, so confirm specific allergen needs directly.
Fully plant-based kitchen means vegans can order anything on the menu with confidence and no animal cross-contact.
Broth is a clean 12-hour kelp, shiitake and vegetable infusion with no fish or meat dashi.
